newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: South Korea reopens door to investment in N.Korea.
newsitem.headline: South Korea reopens door to investment in N.Korea.

text.p: South Korea opened the door for domestic companies to invest in rival North Korea on Friday for the first time since a submarine incursion shut off all contact between the two sides.
The Unification Ministry said it had given approval to seven firms to open talks with North Koreans to develop joint projects ranging from garment making to soft drinks.
All contacts were frozen after a North Korean Shark-class submarine dropped 26 intruders on a Southern beach last September.
Pyongyang issued a rare apology last month for the incident, prompting new progress towards peace talks between the two Koreas, the United States and China.
This week, the South Korean Red Cross said it would resume aid shipments to North Korea and the first consignment of flour and socks would be despatched this month.
The seven firms include Lotte Group, LG International Corp, Shin Won Corp, Korea Green Cross Corp, Taechang Co Ltd and Dong Hae Trading Co.
To initiate talks, South Korean firms usually must meet North Koreans in third countries, such as China, because direct travel is restricted.
The only South Korean firm allowed a permanent presence in North Korea is the giant Daewoo Group. It runs a joint venture textile factory.

But company executives and government officials cautioned that any improvement in economic cooperation would be difficult until overall Korean ties improved, and they ruled out any immediate rush of investment to the North.

"There should first be development in the overall relationship between the two sides before economic ties begin gaining heat," said an official at the Unification Ministry's Inter-Korean Economic Cooperation Department.
"Today's approval was just for contacts, not for any specific project. Our group also has no specific project there yet," said a senior Lotte Group official.
There have been few business deals between the two Koreas, which remain technically at war after their 1950-53 conflict ended in a truce and not a peace agreement.
Seoul first allowed business links with the North in the late 1980s in the hope contact could thaw decades of hostility.
Business projects have so far focused on the processing-on-consignment of garments, bags and sewn goods while North Korea has sold some raw materials to the South.
South Korean approvals for trade and investment with the North fell to $243.06 million last year from $309.83 million in 1995, according to Unification Ministry data.
The Stalinist state's economy has shrunk for six consecutive years, partly due to the collapse of the Soviet Union, its main benefactor for nearly half a century.
North Korea is also suffering severe food shortages after two years of floods. International aid agencies have said the crisis could worsen.
Chronic food shortages have sparked a series of defections to the South, with two families of eight who arrived in Seoul on Wednesday the latest to seek political asylum.
